annotations.text:
THE QUESTION

The lozenge is 226x372 of the best space on the screen and it answers "what is it doing outside right now?" — the one weather question a person standing in their own house can already answer by looking out of a window.

So every direction here is judged on one thing: does it tell you something the window does not?

All five are the same pane, same drawing, same four-line anatomy. Only the words change. Nothing here needs a new shape — if a direction needed one, that would be the argument against it.

WHAT THE HOUSE ACTUALLY KNOWS

Today, from the weather entity: condition, temperature, humidity, wind. That is all brain/hub/api.py reads — `_weather_of()`, four attributes off the current state.

Already in the house, unused here: indoor temperature (every thermostat's current_temperature, every sensor.temperature), open windows and doors (the contact capability), the covers, the thermostat's mode.

NOT fetched at all: any forecast. HA has one behind the `weather.get_forecasts` service, hourly and daily. Nothing in the hub calls it.

So A and C cost panel work only. B and D need that one service call, a forecast field on the ambient payload, and a refresh — real work, but contained, and it is the same call for both.

The rule the panel already holds itself to: WallView.vue refuses to draw "Feels like 81°" because nothing in the house measures it. Nothing on this canvas invents a reading either.

TODAY — what ships

Four lines: the number, the condition, sunset, humidity.

The number and the condition are the window's job. Sunset is charm, and the sky behind the panel is already drawing it. Humidity is the weakest line on the screen — 48% is a fact almost nobody acts on.

Here as the control, not as a straw man: it is a beautiful object, and whatever replaces a line has to be worth more than the calm it costs.

A — INSIDE AND OUT

78 out, 71 in. The comparison is the point: it is the number that makes somebody open a window or close the blinds, and it is the one thing a weather app on a phone can never show, because it is the only one that knows the house.

Costs no hub work at all — the thermostat's reading is already on the panel, one tile away.

Tradeoff: it is still only NOW. And the second number moves the eye off the big one, so the pane stops being readable in one glance from across a room, which is what the size of that numeral is for.

The small caps "Outside" is doing real work here and is worth arguing about — without it the two numbers are just two numbers.

B — WHAT IS COMING  (the leading one)

The change, not the state. "Rain from 4 PM" is the sentence that alters what somebody does in the next hour, and it is the reason a weather display earns wall space at all.

Sunset and humidity both go. The high/low takes the quiet line, because a range is the second thing you want and the first thing you can read at a glance.

It keeps the existing anatomy exactly — four lines, same sizes — so it is the smallest visual change on this canvas and the largest change in usefulness.

Tradeoff: it needs the forecast (see the note far left), and it needs a good answer for the hours when nothing is coming. "Clear through midnight" is the obvious fallback and it is weaker than the line it replaces. Worth deciding before this gets built.

D — THE DAY

The next eight hours as one ribbon: the temperature curve, the rain banded where it falls, three hour marks.

The most information per pixel on the canvas, and the only direction that shows SHAPE — that it warms until two and rains for two hours and clears.

Tradeoff, and it is a real one: a ribbon this small is read at arm's length, and this panel is drawn to be read from across a room. It may simply be the wrong instrument for a wall. Judge this one by walking away from the screen.

Same forecast call as B — if B is built, this is a later refinement of it rather than a separate piece of work.

C — THE HOUSE'S ANSWER

The lozenge does not change at all. The weather's consequence goes to the band instead: rain is coming and two windows are open.

This is the architecturally honest one. WallView.vue is explicit that the weather is "not in the house" — it is scenery, it parallaxes at its own rate, it is deliberately not a card and not tappable. An actionable line inside it fights that, and fights the rule that nothing vanishes under a tap.

The band is already defined as "what Home owes a person" and is already the only route to some things. A weather consequence belongs there.

Tradeoff: it says nothing at all on the ordinary day when the house has no stake in the weather — which is most days. So this is not really an alternative to B. It is the thing to build AFTER B, on top of the same forecast.

THE PANE — tapping the weather

This is the answer to the crowding, and it is a better one than picking between A, B and D.

The pill goes back to being a glance. Everything that wanted a fifth line — the forecast, the day, inside against outside, the house's stake in it — moves here, where it is read at arm's length because you walked over and touched it.

It is the pane every other card already opens: 25vh from the top so the row you came from is still there dimmed above it, 34px on the top corners only, the said column at 560 and the instrument beside it at 32px radius. Nothing new was invented for the weather.

ONE SLOT IS DELIBERATELY EMPTY. Every other pane has a row of verbs under the name. The weather has none — there is nothing to do to it. That is exactly what makes the lozenge safe to make tappable: WallView.vue's objection is that the weather is scenery and must not behave like a control, and a pane with no controls in it does not. Nothing changes under the tap; nothing vanishes under it either.

What it costs: the same forecast call as B and D, plus the pane wiring. The pill itself can then stay exactly as it is today, or take B's one line — that choice stops being urgent once this exists.
